content.content:
runtime:
        The container runtime is Podman, run through the `podman` command,
        and no other. Each run is one `podman run --rm` of the harness's
        command, run as a child of the application, given its prompt on its
        standard input and streaming back what it does on its output, just as
        a run on the host does, so stopping or cancelling a run stops its
        container with it, and nothing is left behind once it is over.

        On Linux, Podman runs rootless, and the container runs as the user,
        with `--userns=keep-id`, so every file a run writes belongs to the
        user, as it would on the host. On macOS and Windows, Podman runs its
        containers in a Podman machine, a virtual machine it manages. There
        too, what a run writes to the project belongs to the user, as the
        @{Application} says of every file the application creates:
        the container runs as the user rather than as root inside the
        machine, and a file it writes into a folder mounted from Windows is
        the user's, owned by them and inheriting the folder's permissions,
        never owned by Administrators or another account.

    missingPodman:

cd /home/hyphyphyph/piton/repl; f=spec/scope/container-environment/index.pi; s=36; e=$(grep -n "^    missingPodman:" $f | cut -d: -f1); head -$((s-1)) $f > /tmp/x; cat >> /tmp/x <<'EOF'
    runtime:
        The container runtime is Podman or Docker, whichever is in use: run
        through the `podman` or the `docker` command, and no other. Each run
        is one `run --rm` of the harness's command by that runtime, run as a
        child of the application, given its prompt on its standard input and
        streaming back what it does on its output, just as a run on the host
        does, so stopping or cancelling a run stops its container with it,
        and nothing is left behind once it is over. Wherever this spec names
        Podman, a `podman` command, or a Podman machine, it means the runtime
        in use, Docker's own equivalent standing in for it while Docker is,
        as below; everything else is the same whichever runs the containers.

    choosingRuntime:
        Which runtime is in use is picked in the Containers section of the
        @{SettingsWindow}: "Automatic", "Podman", or "Docker", Automatic until
        another is picked, remembered for the user, as the @{UserPreferences}
        says, not for a project. Automatic is worked out at each launch, and
        again whenever the settings or the welcome checks look: the first of
        Podman and Docker that is installed and can run a container for the
        user, Podman first where both can, since it runs rootless on Linux.
        Where neither can, nothing is picked, and what needs a container
        fails saying neither is available, with links to install either, as
        a missing Podman does below. Podman or Docker picked by hand is used
        whether or not it is working, and its runs fail saying why where it
        isn't. A run already going when the runtime changes finishes with
        the one it started with; the next run uses the new one, building its
        image there first where it has none.

    userAndFiles:
        On Linux, Podman runs rootless, and the container runs as the user,
        with `--userns=keep-id`; Docker runs the container as the user, with
        `--user` given the user's id and group, and the harness's home a
        directory owned by that id. Either way every file a run writes
        belongs to the user, as it would on the host. On macOS and Windows,
        Podman runs its containers in a Podman machine and Docker in Docker
        Desktop's virtual machine, each a virtual machine the runtime
        manages: where Docker Desktop isn't running, the run says so and
        offers "Start Docker", which starts it, as "Start Podman" does for a
        Podman machine. There too, what a run writes to the project belongs
        to the user, as the @{Application} says of every file the application
        creates: the container runs as the user rather than as root inside
        the machine, and a file it writes into a folder mounted from Windows
        is the user's, owned by them and inheriting the folder's permissions,
        never owned by Administrators or another account. Where this spec
        mounts a volume so the user owns it, with Podman's `:U`, Docker gives
        it to the user\'s id when the application creates it, by a short
        `chown` run in a throwaway container before the volume is first used.

    resources:
        Every container, image, and volume the application makes, with
        whichever runtime, is labelled `io.suspense.app=suspense`, and its
        name begins with `suspense-`, so the application can always find what
        is its own and never touches what isn't. Images are tagged
        `suspense-default` and, for a project with a Containerfile of its
        own, `suspense-project-` and a short hash of the project's path;
        volumes are named `suspense-` and the harness, as `suspense-claude`.
        Runs are always `--rm`, so a container is left only while it runs,
        or where a run was cut off, as by a crash.

EOF
tail -n +$e $f >> /tmp/x; cp /tmp/x $f; sed -i "s/\\\\'/'/g" $f; grep -q "import UserPreferences" $f || sed -i '0,/^from /s#^from #from /scope/user-preferences import UserPreferences\nfrom #' $f; piton check 2>&1|tail -2

        Then "Resources": everything the application has made in either
        runtime, found by its label, as the @{ContainerEnvironment} says,
        listed for each runtime that is installed, Podman's and Docker's
        apart, each under a small heading naming the runtime, with how much
        disk its resources take together. Each resource is a row: an icon for
        its kind, container, image, or volume, its name, muted beside it what
        it is for, as "Default image", "Project image · my-project", "Codex
        login", or "Running: Spec task", its size, and when it was made, then
        a small ghost "Delete" button at its right. Containers come first,
        then images, then volumes. A runtime with nothing of the
        application's reads "Nothing here", muted, and one not installed
        isn't listed.

        `rmi -f`, or `volume rm` do, and the Docker equivalents, after a small
        confirmation saying what is lost: a running container, that the task
        or question running in it is stopped, as cancelling stops it; an
        image, that it is built again when next needed; a harness's volume,
        that the harness must log in again. A "Delete all" button beside each

        the group does so for both runtimes. Deleting never touches anything
        without the application's label, and never a project's own files or
        sessions, which are kept in the project. While a resource is being
        deleted, its row shows a spinner; once it is gone, the row goes, and
        one that couldn't be deleted says why, in the theme's error colour,
        in its row. The list is read anew each time the settings open, and
        a "Refresh" button reads it again.

        without a project open.

content.text:
Suspense now supports Docker as well as Podman, picks whichever is available, and lists its own container resources in Settings so you can delete them. `piton check` reports no problems and `piton build` wrote 84 files.

- **Runtime** (`.claude/reference/scope/container-environment/index.md#runtime`, `#choosing-runtime`):
  - **Choosing:** containers run with Podman or Docker. Settings offers Automatic, Podman or Docker. Automatic picks whichever works at launch, preferring Podman when both do, and the choice is remembered for you.
  - **Same rules either way:** everywhere else the spec says Podman now means whichever runtime is in use, with Docker's equivalents.
  - **Running as you:** on Linux, Docker containers run as your user ID, and its login volumes are handed to you with a one-off `chown`.
  - **Docker Desktop:** on macOS and Windows it stands in for the Podman machine, with a "Start Docker" button.
- **Labelling** (`#resources`): every container, image and volume Suspense creates is labelled `io.suspense.app=suspense` and named `suspense-…`. Suspense only ever touches resources with that label.
- **Settings → Containers** (`.claude/reference/scope/settings-window/index.md#containers`):
  - **Runtime choice:** a picker, plus a status row for each of Podman and Docker.
  - **Resources:** a list per installed runtime with total disk use. Each container, image and volume shows what it's for, its size, its age, and a Delete button.
  - **Deleting:** "Delete all" works per runtime or for both. Every delete is confirmed and says what's lost: a running task stops, an image gets rebuilt, a login volume means logging in again.
- **Welcome checks:** they accept either runtime.

**My choices:** preferring Podman under Automatic, and the label and name scheme. Both are easy to change.

**Anchors the code should follow:** `ContainerEnvironment` `#runtime`, `#choosing-runtime`, `#user-and-files` and `#resources`; `SettingsWindow` `#containers`; `Welcome`'s container checks; and `UserPreferences`.
